VEGETABLE GARDEN PLANTING CALENDAR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Your vegetable garden planting calendar, from two frost dates

Enter your average last spring frost and first fall frost, tick the crops you want, and get every date in order: when to start seeds indoors, when to transplant or sow, how often to make succession plantings, when a fall garden can go in, when to plant garlic, and when the first harvest arrives. Put it in your phone as a calendar file.

New to this? Read when to start seeds indoors, with worked dates.

1. Your frost dates

Find the two frost dates for your town from your local cooperative extension service or a regional frost-date table. In the southern hemisphere enter the spring date and the next autumn's date; the page treats an earlier fall date as next year's. Leave the hot-weather date blank to assume about ten weeks after the last frost.

2. Your crops

Leafy greens and herbs
Roots and alliums
Cabbage family
Peas and beans
Tomatoes, peppers and other fruiting crops
Vines, squash and corn

Enter both frost dates and choose crops, then click Build.

Your plan

Coming up in the next 30 days

    Month by month

    S start indoorsP plant or transplantH harvest

    Every date, in order

    DateWhat to do

    Notes for your crops

    How it is built

    Timing rules: each crop carries a planting date measured in weeks before or after your average last spring frost (hardy crops go in four to six weeks early, tender ones a week or two after), the weeks of indoor head start for transplants, and the days from planting to first harvest. These are common extension-service rules of thumb.

    Succession and the end of the season: sowings repeat at the crop's interval until there is no longer time to mature before the first fall frost (hardy crops get four weeks of grace, half-hardy two, tender none). Cool-season crops also stop before summer heat and get a second window in late summer for a fall harvest, with two extra weeks allowed because autumn days are shorter.

    Dates, not a forecast: the plan is for a typical year. A cold spring or an early frost moves everything, so treat each date as a target and watch the weather.

    Checked: the test suite builds plans for dozens of frost-date combinations and every crop and confirms that no tender crop is planned before the last frost, no planting is too late to mature, cool crops finish before the heat, and dates always run in order.

    Common questions

    How do I find my last frost date?

    Look up the average last spring frost and average first fall frost for your town from your local cooperative extension service, a regional frost-date table or an almanac, and enter them here. They are averages, so some years the last frost comes a week or two later. Choose the cautious setting if a late frost has caught you before.

    When should I start tomato seeds indoors?

    About six weeks before you plan to move the seedlings outside, and the move itself happens about a week after your average last frost. With a last frost on May 1 that means starting seeds around March 27 and transplanting around May 8. Peppers and eggplant like a longer head start of about eight weeks.

    What does succession planting mean?

    Sowing a small amount every couple of weeks instead of everything at once, so lettuce, radishes, beans and carrots arrive a few at a time instead of all in one week. The calendar lists each sowing date for the crops where this pays off and stops when there is no longer time to mature before frost.

    Why does lettuce stop in summer and start again in late summer?

    Lettuce, spinach, radish, broccoli and other cool-season crops bolt or turn bitter in hot weather. The calendar stops spring sowing early enough to finish before the heat, then offers a second planting window in late summer for a fall harvest. You can set the date hot weather usually starts where you live.

    Does this work in the southern hemisphere?

    Yes. Enter your last frost in spring (for example September 30) and your first frost in autumn (for example June 1 of the next calendar year). When the fall frost date falls before the spring one, the page treats it as the following year, so the plan runs across New Year.

    Can I put the dates in my phone calendar?

    Yes. Download the calendar file and open it in Google Calendar, Apple Calendar or Outlook. Every sowing, transplanting and first-harvest date becomes an all-day event. You can also download a CSV for a spreadsheet or copy the plan as plain text.

    Is my garden plan uploaded anywhere?

    No. The calculation runs in your browser, nothing is sent to a server and there are no accounts. Use Save plan if you want a file to load again next season.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is general gardening guidance, not agricultural, horticultural, legal or financial advice, and it is not a forecast. You are responsible for checking your local frost dates, weather and your seed packet's instructions before you plant. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss, including lost plants or crops, arising from its use.

    Independent. Not affiliated with any seed company, extension service, almanac or gardening brand, and none is named or ranked here.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere, so use Save plan and keep the file.

    Everything runs in your browser. Your dates and crop choices are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (plan_built, example_loaded, ics_downloaded, csv_downloaded, text_copied, file_saved) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.

    Related tools: the market garden bed planner for choosing a crop mix under bed and labor limits, and the greenhouse bench planner for seedling bench space.

    Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

when-to-start-seeds-indoors.html.text:
← Vegetable garden planting calendar

When to start seeds indoors, with a worked example

Every seed-starting date is counted from one number: your average last spring frost. Cold-hardy crops go out before it, tender ones after it, and the head start indoors is worked backwards from the day you plan to plant them out. This page works through seven crops for a garden whose average last frost is May 1.

Build your own calendar for free

The method

Pick the day the seedling goes outside (the transplant date), then subtract the weeks it needs indoors. Tomatoes go out about a week after the last frost and want six weeks inside. Peppers and eggplant go out two weeks after and want eight weeks. Broccoli and cabbage tolerate light frost, so they go out two weeks before the last frost after six weeks indoors.

Seven crops, last frost May 1

CropStart seeds indoorsTransplant outsideFirst harvest
TomatoMar 27May 8Jul 17
PepperMar 20May 15Jul 24
EggplantMar 20May 15Jul 29
BroccoliMar 6Apr 17Jun 26
CabbageMar 6Apr 17Jul 1
BasilApr 10May 15Jun 14
WatermelonApr 24May 15Aug 3

Harvest dates count from the transplant date using typical days to maturity. Basil is shown with its first cutting, not a full harvest.

Where the last frost date comes from

It is an average: in about half of years the real last frost comes after it. That is why tender seedlings wait a week or two past the date, and why the calendar has a cautious setting that adds a week more. Your local cooperative extension service or a regional frost-date table gives the average for your town.
